summary: The Letters Patent, 1947 is a legal instrument issued by King George VI that took effect on 1 October 1947 and, together with parts of the Constitution Act, 1867, constitutes the Office of the Governor General of Canada. It expands the governor general's role in exercising the Royal Prerogative, allowing them to perform more of the Sovereign's duties in exceptional circumstances. The powers remain with the monarch, who can revoke, alter, or amend the permission at any time, and the governor general exercises them on the monarch's behalf.
one_line: A 1947 legal instrument by King George VI that, with parts of the Constitution Act, 1867, constitutes the Office of Governor General of Canada.
key_facts: The Letters Patent, 1947 is formally titled the Letters Patent Constituting the Office of Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of Canada.
The Letters Patent, 1947 was introduced by King George VI.
The Letters Patent, 1947 came into effect on 1 October 1947.
The Letters Patent, 1947, together with parts of the Constitution Act, 1867, constitutes the Office of the Governor General.
The Letters Patent, 1947 expands the role and powers of the governor general in exercising the Royal Prerogative.
The Letters Patent, 1947 allows the governor general to carry out an increased number of the Sovereign's duties in "exceptional circumstances".
The Letters Patent, 1947 permits the governor general to use most of the "powers and authorities" lawfully belonging to the Canadian sovereign.
The sovereign can revoke, alter, or amend the permission granted by the Letters Patent, 1947 at any time.
Powers and authorities under the Letters Patent, 1947 remain with the monarch and are carried out by the governor general on the monarch's behalf.
